11.section: Art. EDPS TechDispatch #3/2025; cryptographic literature (Chaum, Camenisch)
11.content: A family of privacy-preserving cryptographic mechanisms that support both selective disclosure and unlinkability requirements. Anonymous credentials enable authentication without identification when identification is not strictly necessary, using advanced cryptographic techniques such as Camenisch-Lysyanskaya (CL) signatures or BBS+ signatures to provide mathematical proof of a claim without disclosing any additional information. The term 'anonymous' refers to the ability to minimise data disclosure, not necessarily full anonymity in the broader context.

20.content: a characteristic, quality, right or permission of a natural or legal person or of an object | A characteristic, quality, right, or permission of a natural or legal person or of an object. In the EUDI Wallet ecosystem, attributes are the fundamental units of information that are issued, stored, and presented through electronic attestations. They encompass a wide range of data: from person identification data (name, date of birth, nationality) to professional qualifications, health credentials, driving licences, and organisational permissions. Attributes are structured within namespaces that define their identifier, syntax, and semantics (ARF Annex 1 Section A.4), and are governed by attestation rulebooks that specify their encoding formats and issuance requirements (ARF Topic 12). During presentation, wallet users may selectively disclose individual attributes rather than the entire attestation (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(4)), and relying parties shall not request attributes beyond those registered for their intended purpose (eIDAS Art. 5b(3)). Attributes may be issued from authentic sources — repositories held by public or private entities recognised as authoritative for that information (eIDAS Art. 3(47)).

67.content: the method to link person identification data or electronic attestations of attributes to wallet units through cryptographic means | The method used to link person identification data or electronic attestations of attributes to a wallet unit, ensuring that a credential can only be presented by the wallet unit to which it was issued. This is achieved by cryptographically tying the attestation to public keys whose corresponding private keys are protected within the wallet unit's WSCD (wallet secure cryptographic device). Specifically: (1) during issuance, the PID provider or attestation provider binds the credential to one or more public keys generated by the wallet unit's WSCA and protected by its WSCD (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 5, 6); (2) during presentation, the wallet unit proves possession of the corresponding private keys to the relying party, demonstrating that the credential has not been transferred to another device (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(3)); (3) the binding must follow the cryptographic standards listed in CIR 2024/2979 Annex II, which specify the acceptable signature schemes, key types, and binding mechanisms; and (4) the binding mechanism must be resistant to attackers with high attack potential, as required by the national certification schemes (CIR 2024/2981 Annex IV). Cryptographic binding is distinct from device binding (which ties credentials to the physical device) and is the primary mechanism preventing credential cloning, transfer, and replay attacks in the EUDI Wallet ecosystem.

83.section: Art. What is the difference between an electronic signature and a digital signature?
83.content: A digital signature refers to a mathematical and cryptographic concept that is widely used to provide concrete and practical instances of electronic signature. The definition given by ETSI TR 119 100 is that of data appended to, or a cryptographic transformation of a data unit that allows a recipient of the data unit to prove the source and integrity of the data unit and protect against forgery e.g. by the recipient. These two concepts should be distinguished, as all electronic signatures are not necessarily digital signatures.

93.content: EAA an attestation in electronic form that allows attributes to be authenticated | An attestation in electronic form that allows attributes to be authenticated — a verifiable digital credential containing a set of attributes (characteristics, qualities, rights, or permissions) about a natural or legal person. Electronic attestations of attributes (EAAs) are the general credential type in the EUDI Wallet ecosystem and exist in three tiers: (1) Qualified EAAs (QEAAs), issued by qualified trust service providers and meeting the requirements of eIDAS Annex V, with the same legal effect as legally issued paper attestations (eIDAS Art. 45f); (2) EAAs issued by or on behalf of public sector bodies (PuB-EAAs), issued from authentic sources with equivalent recognition (eIDAS Art. 45f); and (3) non-qualified EAAs, which may be issued by any provider. Providers issuing EAAs to wallet units must identify themselves using wallet-relying party access certificates (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 4(2)) and ensure that attestations contain the information necessary for authentication and validation (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 4(3)). EAAs shall be cryptographically bound to the wallet unit using the standards in CIR 2024/2979 Annex II, and providers may embed disclosure policies specifying conditions that relying parties must meet to access the attestation (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 11, CIR 2024/2982 Art. 2(13)). Wallet users can selectively disclose individual attributes from an EAA without revealing the full credential (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(4)).

105.content: data in electronic form, which is attached to or logically associated with other data in electronic form to ensure the latter’s origin and integrity | An electronic seal is a data in electronic form, which is attached to or logically associated with other data in electronic form to ensure the latter's origin and integrity, where the creator of a seal is a legal person (unlike the electronic signature that is issued by a natural person). Electronic seals might serve as evidence that an electronic document was issued by a legal person, ensuring certainty of the document's origin and integrity. | Data in electronic form, which is attached to or logically associated with other data in electronic form to ensure the latter's origin and integrity. Electronic seals are the organisational counterpart of electronic signatures — where signatures are for natural persons, seals are for legal persons (organisations). The eIDAS Regulation establishes a parallel three-tier hierarchy: (1) simple electronic seals, which shall not be denied legal effect solely because they are in electronic form (eIDAS Art. 35(1)); (2) advanced electronic seals, which must be uniquely linked to and capable of identifying the creator, created using data under the creator's high degree of confidence, and linked to the sealed data so that changes are detectable (eIDAS Art. 36); and (3) qualified electronic seals, which enjoy a presumption of integrity and correctness of origin across all Member States (eIDAS Art. 35(2)). In the EUDI Wallet ecosystem, electronic seals play critical infrastructure roles: wallet unit attestations are signed or sealed by wallet providers (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 3(2)), wallet-relying party access certificates are certificates for seals or signatures (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 3(12)), and attestation providers seal the credentials they issue to wallet units (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 4).

106.content: unique data, which is used by the creator of the electronic seal to create an electronic seal

108.content: data in electronic form which is attached to or logically associated with other data in electronic form and which is used by the signatory to sign | An electronic signature is a data in electronic form which is attached to or logically associated with other data in electronic form and which is used by the signatory to sign, where the signatory is a natural person. Like its handwritten counterpart in the offline world, an electronic signature can be used, for instance, to electronically indicate that the signatory has written the document, agreed with the content of the document, or that the signatory was present as a witness. | Data in electronic form which is attached to or logically associated with other data in electronic form and which is used by the signatory to sign. The eIDAS Regulation establishes a three-tier hierarchy of electronic signatures with increasing legal strength: (1) simple electronic signatures, which shall not be denied legal effect solely because they are in electronic form (eIDAS Art. 25(1)); (2) advanced electronic signatures, which must be uniquely linked to and capable of identifying the signatory, created using data under the signatory's sole control, and linked to the signed data so that any subsequent change is detectable (eIDAS Art. 26); and (3) qualified electronic signatures, created by a qualified signature creation device and based on a qualified certificate, which have the legal effect equivalent to handwritten signatures across all Member States (eIDAS Art. 25(2-3)). In the EUDI Wallet context, wallet users who are natural persons must have free-of-charge access to qualified electronic signature creation for non-professional purposes (eIDAS Art. 5a(2)), with the wallet interfacing with local, external, or remote QSCDs for key operations (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 12).

111.content: data in electronic form which binds other data in electronic form to a particular time establishing evidence that the latter data existed at that time | An electronic time stamp is a data in electronic form which binds other data in electronic form to a particular time establishing evidence that the latter data existed at that time. For example, a signatory can use an electronic time stamp to bind a signed document to a particular date and time and prove in the future that the signed document existed at this particular date and time.

112.content: a set of rules, embedded in an electronic attestation of attributes by its provider, that indicates the conditions that a wallet-relying party has to meet to access the electronic attestation of attributes | a set of rules, embedded in an electronic attestation of attributes by its provider, that indicates the conditions that a wallet-relying party has to meet to access the electronic attestation of attributes | a set of rules, embedded in an electronic attestation of attributes by its provider, that indicates the conditions that a wallet-relying party has to meet to access the electronic attestation of attributes | A set of rules, embedded in an electronic attestation of attributes by its provider, that indicates the conditions that a wallet-relying party has to meet to access the electronic attestation of attributes. Embedded disclosure policies are a privacy-by-design mechanism that allows attestation providers to enforce access controls beyond what the wallet user alone decides. Key aspects include: (1) the policy is embedded at issuance time and travels with the attestation throughout its lifecycle (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 11); (2) wallet providers must implement mechanisms to evaluate and enforce these policies during presentation flows, ensuring that relying parties meet the specified conditions before attributes are disclosed (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 11); (3) the conditions may restrict which categories of relying parties may access the attestation, based on their registered purpose or sector (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 2(13)); (4) the wallet instance must inform the user about the embedded policy and its implications before presenting the attestation (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(5)); and (5) embedded disclosure policies work in conjunction with, not as a replacement for, the user's own consent — the user retains final control over whether to share the attestation (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(4)).

180.content: LoA The degree of confidence in the claimed identity of a person when using electronic identification. The EUDIW must comply with High LoA standards for storing and presenting qualified attestations.

181.section: Art. What is the List of Trusted Lists (LOTL)?

228.content: PID a set of data that is issued in accordance with Union or national law and that enables the establishment of the identity of a natural or legal person, or of a natural person representing another natural person or a legal person | A set of data that is issued in accordance with Union or national law and that enables the establishment of the identity of a natural or legal person, or of a natural person representing another natural person or a legal person. Person identification data (PID) is the foundational credential in the EUDI Wallet ecosystem — every wallet unit must contain at least one valid PID before it can be used for other operations (eIDAS Art. 5a(4)(d)). Key aspects include: (1) PID is issued exclusively by Member States (or entities mandated by them) and constitutes the authoritative digital identity of the holder (eIDAS Art. 5a(12)); (2) it must be issued free of charge to every natural person who requests it (eIDAS Art. 5a(16)); (3) PID must be cryptographically bound to the wallet unit via the WSCD, preventing transfer to another wallet (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 5-6); (4) PID providers must identify themselves to the wallet unit using wallet-relying party access certificates before issuance (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 4(2)); (5) the minimum mandatory PID attributes include current family name(s), current first name(s), date of birth, and a unique persistent identifier, with optional attributes such as nationality, address, and document metadata specified by the Commission (eIDAS Art. 5a(13)); and (6) PID supports selective disclosure, allowing users to present only a subset of their identity attributes (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(4)).

242.content: A presentation interaction where the Relying Party and the Wallet Unit communicate in close physical range — typically via BLE, NFC, or QR code — without requiring internet connectivity for the data exchange itself. Proximity flows follow ISO/IEC 18013-5 and are designed for in-person verification scenarios such as border control, age verification, or physical access. Support for proximity flows is not mandatory per the ARF but may be required by specific Attestation Rulebooks (EW-DM-12-003).

243.content: Data uniquely representing a User which in itself does not allow inference of the User's attributes or person identification data, without additional information kept separately by the issuer of the data.

244.content: the processing of personal data in such a manner that the personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organisational measures to ensure that the personal data are not attributed to an identified or identifiable natural person

245.content: an entity recognised as such in a Member State in accordance with national law, not including the judiciary, parliaments or central banks, which complies with the following criteria:

246.content: any government or other public administration entity, including national central banks

247.content: a public electronic communications network as defined in Article 2, point (8), of Directive (EU) 2018/1972

248.content: PKI Systems, software, and communication protocols that are used by EUDI Wallet ecosystem components to distribute, manage, and control public keys. A PKI publishes public keys and establishes trust within an environment by validating and verifying the public keys mapping to an entity.

249.content: A fixed legal phrase indicating that a provision applies regardless of whether the entity or sector involved is part of government/public administration (public) or commercial/non-governmental (private). Used to ensure equal treatment and applicability across all sectors.

250.content: a state, regional or local authority, a body governed by public law or an association formed by one or several such authorities or one or several such bodies governed by public law, or a private entity mandated by at least one of those authorities, bodies or associations to provide public services, when acting under such a mandate

251.content: A legal phrase meaning "in accordance with" or "as authorized by." It indicates that an action is taken based on the authority granted by a specific legal provision. Example: "pursuant to Article 24" means the action is authorized or required by that article.

252.content: QC stands for a qualified certificate. As part of eIDAS, a qualified certificate can either be a: Qualified certificate for electronic signature, Qualified certificate for electronic seal, or Qualified certificate for website authentication.

253.content: QES is the acronym for either qualified electronic signature or qualified electronic seal. It is the third and most secure level of electronic signature/seal defined in eIDAS.

254.content: QSCD stands for a qualified electronic signature/seal creation device.

255.content: a certificate for an electronic seal, that is issued by a qualified trust service provider and meets the requirements laid down in Annex III

256.content: a certificate for electronic signatures, that is issued by a qualified trust service provider and meets the requirements laid down in Annex I

257.content: a certificate for website authentication, which is issued by a qualified trust service provider and meets the requirements laid down in Annex IV

258.content: a distributed electronic ledger that meets the requirements of a qualified electronic ledger

259.content: an electronic archiving service which is provided by a qualified trust service provider and which meets the requirements laid down in Article 45j

260.term: Qualified Electronic Attestation of Attributes QEAA
260.termLower: qualified electronic attestation of attributes qeaa
260.content: QEAA an electronic attestation of attributes which is issued by a qualified trust service provider and meets the requirements laid down in Annex V | An electronic attestation of attributes which is issued by a qualified trust service provider and meets the requirements laid down in Annex V of the eIDAS Regulation. Qualified EAAs (QEAAs) represent the highest tier of verifiable credentials in the EUDI Wallet ecosystem and carry enhanced legal effects: they shall have the same legal effect as lawfully issued attestations in paper form (eIDAS Art. 45f(1)), and QEAAs issued in one Member State shall be recognised in all other Member States (eIDAS Art. 45f(2)). To achieve qualified status, the issuing QTSP must: (1) verify the attributes against authentic sources or equivalent authoritative records (eIDAS Annex V); (2) verify the identity of the person to whom the attestation is issued (eIDAS Art. 45d(2)); (3) include mandatory metadata such as the issuer identity, issuance and expiry dates, attestation type, and the scheme under which it was issued (eIDAS Annex V); (4) cryptographically bind the attestation to the wallet unit using standards from CIR 2024/2979 Annex II; and (5) provide mechanisms for verifying the attestation's validity status, including revocation checking (eIDAS Art. 45e). QTSPs issuing QEAAs must hold a valid wallet-relying party access certificate to identify themselves to wallet units during issuance (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 4(2)).

261.content: an electronic ledger which is provided by a qualified trust service provider and which meets the requirements laid down in Article 45l

262.content: an electronic registered delivery service which meets the requirements laid down in Article 44

263.content: an advanced electronic seal, which is created by a qualified electronic seal creation device, and that is based on a qualified certificate for electronic seal | A qualified electronic seal is an advanced electronic seal which is additionally: created by a qualified seal creation device (QSCD); and is based on a qualified certificate for electronic seals. | An advanced electronic seal, which is created by a qualified electronic seal creation device, and that is based on a qualified certificate for electronic seal. Qualified electronic seals are the organisational equivalent of qualified electronic signatures — they provide the strongest level of integrity and origin assurance for data sealed by legal persons. A QESeal enjoys a presumption of integrity of the data and of correctness of the origin of the data to which it is linked (eIDAS Art. 35(2)), and when issued in one Member State it shall be recognised in all others (eIDAS Art. 35(3)). In the EUDI Wallet ecosystem, qualified electronic seals are integral to the trust infrastructure: (1) wallet unit attestations (WUAs) are signed or sealed by wallet providers using qualified certificates (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 3(2)); (2) PID providers and attestation providers seal the credentials they issue (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 4); and (3) wallet-relying party access certificates may be certificates for electronic seals (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 3(12)).

264.content: an electronic seal creation device that meets mutatis mutandis the requirements laid down in Annex II

265.content: QES an advanced electronic signature that is created by a qualified electronic signature creation device, and which is based on a qualified certificate for electronic signatures | A qualified electronic signature is an advanced electronic signature which is additionally: created by a qualified signature creation device (QSCD); and is based on a qualified certificate for electronic signatures. | An advanced electronic signature that is created by a qualified electronic signature creation device, and which is based on a qualified certificate for electronic signatures. Qualified electronic signatures represent the highest level of electronic signing under eIDAS and carry the legal equivalence of handwritten signatures (eIDAS Art. 25(2)). A QES issued in one Member State shall be recognised as such in all other Member States (eIDAS Art. 25(3)). In the EUDI Wallet context: (1) every wallet must provide access to qualified electronic signature creation functionality for natural persons, free of charge for non-professional purposes (eIDAS Art. 5a(2)); (2) the wallet may use a local QSCD (embedded in the user's device), an external QSCD (e.g. a smartcard), or a remote QSCD managed by a qualified trust service provider (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 12); (3) the QSCD must meet the requirements of eIDAS Annex II and be certified accordingly (eIDAS Art. 29-30); and (4) the wallet provider must ensure the registration of the user's identity by a QTSP before issuing qualified certificates for signatures (eIDAS Art. 24(1)).

266.content: an electronic signature creation device that meets the requirements laid down in Annex II

267.content: an electronic time stamp which meets the requirements laid down in Article 42 | Following stricter requirements laid down in eIDAS, a qualified electronic time stamp enjoys the presumption of the accuracy of the date and the time it indicates and the integrity of the data (e.g. signed document) to which the date and time are bound.

268.section: Art. What is a qualified signature/seal creation device (QSCD)?
268.content: QSealCD A qualified signature/seal creation device (QSCD), by following stricter requirements laid down in eIDAS, offers higher guarantees regarding the protection (e.g. mitigating any kind of replication or forgery) of the electronic signature/seal creation data (such as the private key) and therefore higher legal certainty regarding the created qualified electronic signatures/seals.

269.section: Art. What is a qualified signature/seal creation device (QSCD)?
269.content: QSCD A qualified signature/seal creation device (QSCD), by following stricter requirements laid down in eIDAS, offers higher guarantees regarding the protection (e.g. mitigating any kind of replication or forgery) of the electronic signature/seal creation data (such as the private key) and therefore higher legal certainty regarding the created qualified electronic signatures/seals.

270.content: a trust service that meets the applicable requirements laid down in this Regulation | a qualified trust service as defined in Article 3, point (17), of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 | Qualified trust services are subject to strict requirements that consist of: (a) Issuing qualified certificates for electronic signature, electronic seal, and website authentication; (b) Providing qualified validation of qualified electronic signature and qualified electronic seal; (c) Providing qualified preservation of qualified electronic signature and qualified electronic seal; (d) Issuing qualified time stamp; (e) Providing qualified electronic registered delivery. | A trust service that meets the applicable requirements laid down in the eIDAS Regulation. Qualified status is the regulatory quality mark that elevates a trust service to the highest tier of legal recognition. To achieve and maintain qualified status: (1) the trust service provider must undergo a conformity assessment by an accredited conformity assessment body (eIDAS Art. 20-21); (2) the service must be listed in the national Trusted List published by the Member State (eIDAS Art. 22); (3) the service must comply with the specific requirements laid down for each service type — qualified certificates for electronic signatures (eIDAS Art. 28, Annex I), qualified certificates for electronic seals (eIDAS Art. 38, Annex III), qualified time stamps (eIDAS Art. 42), qualified electronic registered delivery (eIDAS Art. 44), qualified website authentication certificates (eIDAS Art. 45a), qualified electronic attestations of attributes (eIDAS Art. 45d-45e), qualified electronic archiving (eIDAS Art. 45g), and qualified electronic ledgers (eIDAS Art. 45i); and (4) qualified trust services shall be recognised across all Member States without additional requirements, ensuring cross-border interoperability. The distinction between qualified and non-qualified services fundamentally affects legal effect: qualified electronic signatures have handwritten-equivalent status (eIDAS Art. 25(2)), qualified seals enjoy a presumption of integrity (eIDAS Art. 35(2)), and QEAAs have the legal effect of lawfully issued paper attestations (eIDAS Art. 45f(1)).

271.content: QTSP a trust service provider who provides one or more qualified trust services and is granted the qualified status by the supervisory body | a qualified trust service provider as defined in Article 3, point (20), of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 | A qualified trust service provider (QTSP) is a TSP who provides one or more qualified trust services (QTS) and is granted the qualified status by the national supervisory body. The decision of the supervisory body to grant the qualified status is reflected in the corresponding national Trusted List. In this respect, QTSPs are mandatorily listed in the corresponding national Trusted List while TSP could be but are not mandatorily listed in these Trusted Lists. | A trust service provider who provides one or more qualified trust services and is granted the qualified status by the supervisory body. Qualified trust service providers (QTSPs) occupy the highest tier of trust in the eIDAS framework and must: (1) undergo an initial conformity assessment by an accredited conformity assessment body before commencing operations, then be assessed at least every 24 months thereafter (eIDAS Art. 20(1)); (2) submit a conformity assessment report to the supervisory body, which grants or withdraws qualified status (eIDAS Art. 21(1)); (3) be listed in the national Trusted List published by the Member State as providing qualified trust services (eIDAS Art. 22); (4) bear financial liability for damage caused to any person due to failure to comply with eIDAS obligations, with the burden of proof placed on the QTSP to demonstrate it did not act negligently (eIDAS Art. 13); (5) use trustworthy systems and products protected against modification, ensure that personal data can be processed only with consent or other legal basis, and take appropriate measures against forgery and theft (eIDAS Art. 24(2)); (6) maintain a termination plan to ensure continuity of service and inform the supervisory body at least three months before ceasing operations (eIDAS Art. 24(2)(h-i)); and (7) in the context of the EUDI Wallet, issue qualified electronic attestations of attributes (QEAAs), qualified certificates for electronic signatures and seals, and other qualified trust services (eIDAS Art. 45d-45e).

272.section: Art. eIDAS Article 30, general EU certification practice
272.content: The process of renewing or revalidating a certification after it expires, or when significant changes occur that may affect compliance. Recertification ensures continued adherence to applicable requirements over time. In eIDAS, qualified electronic signature creation devices must be recertified periodically (typically every 5 years, with vulnerability assessments every 2 years per Article 30).

275.content: the body responsible for establishing and maintaining the list of registered wallet-relying parties established in their territory who has been designated by a Member State | the body responsible for establishing and maintaining the list of registered wallet-relying parties established in their territory and who has been designated by a Member State

280.content: RP a natural or legal person that relies upon electronic identification, European Digital Identity Wallets or other electronic identification means, or upon a trust service | A natural or legal person that relies upon electronic identification, European Digital Identity Wallets or other electronic identification means, or upon a trust service. Relying parties that specifically intend to interact with EUDI Wallet Units are termed wallet-relying parties and are subject to additional registration, authentication, and data-minimisation obligations (see wallet-relying party). Intermediaries acting on behalf of relying parties are deemed to be relying parties themselves and shall not store personal data exchanged during the interaction (eIDAS Art. 5b(10)). Public sector relying parties shall accept wallets within 24 months of the implementing acts entering into force; private sector relying parties in regulated sectors shall accept them within 36 months, upon voluntary user request (eIDAS Art. 5b(10), 5c(2)).

281.content: A software and/or hardware module with the capability to interact with a Wallet Unit and to perform Relying Party authentication, that is controlled by a Relying Party.

282.section: Art. Synthesized from ARF Topic 6, OID4VP specification, CIR 2024/2982 Art 5
282.content: A presentation interaction where the Relying Party and the Wallet Unit communicate over the internet, typically using the OID4VP (OpenID for Verifiable Presentations) protocol. Remote flows are the default interaction model for online services — the RP sends a presentation request via HTTPS and receives the VP Token containing the disclosed attributes. All EUDI Wallet Units must support remote flows as the baseline presentation mechanism.

283.section: Art. What is a qualified signature/seal creation device (QSCD)?
283.content: A QSCD is not necessarily in the physical possession of the signatory/creator of the seal but can also be remotely managed by a qualified trust service provider (QTSP). This kind of QSCD is known as "remote QSCD". Those remote QSCD offer an improved user experience while maintaining the legal certainty offered by qualified electronic signatures/seals.

284.term: Remote Qualified Electronic Seal Creation Device rQSealCD

293.content: A microprocessor chip engineered to store sensitive data and perform critical cryptographic operations while offering lower exposure to threats. Secure elements act as hardware vaults, protecting applications and cryptographic key material from malware attacks on the host operating system. Examples include SIM cards, embedded SIMs (eSIMs), embedded secure elements (eSEs), and external security tokens or smart cards.

296.content: SD The capability enabling the User to present a subset of the attributes included in a PID or attestation, rather than disclosing the entire credential. This feature reinforces the protection of personal data and the principle of data minimisation.

298.content: A legal phrase creating a legal fiction or presumption. It establishes that something is legally treated as true or equivalent to something else, regardless of actual facts. Example: "shall be deemed to comply" means the entity is legally presumed compliant if certain conditions are met, even without further verification.

299.content: a natural person who creates an electronic signature

300.content: a cyber threat the technical characteristics of which indicate that it could have the potential to result in a major ICT-related incident or a major operational or security payment-related incident | a cyber threat which, based on its technical characteristics, can be assumed to have the potential to have a severe impact on the network and information systems of an entity or the users of the entity’s services by causing considerable material or non-material damage

301.content: An electronic seal is defined as "data in electronic form, which is attached to or logically associated with other data in electronic form to ensure the latter's origin and integrity".

302.content: An electronic signature is defined as "data in electronic form which is attached to or logically associated with other data in electronic form and which is used by the signatory to sign". Thus, something as simple as writing your name under an e-mail might constitute an electronic signature.

309.section: Art. synthesized from PSD2 Article 4(30), RTS 2018/389, and TS12
309.content: SCA Authentication based on the use of two or more elements categorised as knowledge (something only the user knows), possession (something only the user possesses), and inherence (something the user is) that are independent, in that the breach of one does not compromise the reliability of the others, and is designed in such a way as to protect the confidentiality of the authentication data. Abbreviated as SCA. This is the PSD2-specific term for strong authentication in payment services, defined in PSD2 Article 4(30) and elaborated in the RTS on SCA (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389). SCA goes beyond basic two-factor authentication by additionally requiring Dynamic Linking (binding the authentication to a specific transaction amount and payee), authentication code generation, and transaction monitoring, as mandated by PSD2 Article 97 and the RTS. While functionally equivalent to Strong User Authentication (SUA) in its core two-factor requirement, SCA applies exclusively to payment services and imposes stricter obligations. The EUDI Wallet bridges the gap between SUA and SCA through dedicated SCA Attestations, specified in Technical Specification 12 (TS12), which are issued by Payment Service Providers into Wallet Units and enable Dynamic Linking via transactional data signing.

310.content: SUA an authentication based on the use of at least two authentication factors from different categories of either knowledge, something only the user knows, possession, something only the user possesses or inherence, something the user is, that are independent, in that the breach of one does not compromise the reliability of the others, and is designed in such a way as to protect the confidentiality of the authentication data | Authentication based on the use of at least two authentication factors from different categories of either knowledge (something only the user knows), possession (something only the user possesses), or inherence (something the user is), that are independent, in that the breach of one does not compromise the reliability of the others, and is designed in such a way as to protect the confidentiality of the authentication data. Abbreviated as SUA. Defined in eIDAS 2.0 Article 3(51), this is the generic cross-sector term for strong authentication in the European Digital Identity Framework. Article 5f(2) mandates that private relying parties in regulated sectors (banking, transport, energy, health, telecommunications, etc.) must accept the EUDI Wallet where strong user authentication for online identification is required by EU or national law or by contractual obligation. The EUDI Wallet natively satisfies SUA requirements through its LoA High assurance level. For the payment services sector specifically, the PSD2-specific variant Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) applies, which imposes additional requirements such as Dynamic Linking and authentication codes beyond the base SUA two-factor model.

311.content: An attestation used for strong user authentication in the context of electronic payments, such that when a Relying Party sends a presentation request to a Wallet Unit, it includes transactional data in the request.

312.content: a subsidiary undertaking within the meaning of Article 2, point (10), and Article 22 of Directive 2013/34/EU

315.content: a document that prescribes technical requirements to be fulfilled by a product, process or service | a document that prescribes technical requirements to be fulfilled by a product, process, service or system and which lays down one or more of the following: (a) the characteristics required of a product including levels of quality, performance, interoperability, environmental protection, health, safety or dimensions, and including the requirements applicable to the product as regards the name under which the product is sold, terminology, symbols, testing and test methods, packaging, marking or labelling and conformity assessment procedures | a document that prescribes the technical requirements to be met by, or conformity assessment procedures relating to, an ICT product, ICT service or ICT process | a technical specification as defined in Article 2, point (4), of Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012

316.content: The dates (and possibly times) from and up to which an attestation is technically valid, represented as metadata of the attestation. All PIDs and attestations have a technical validity period, which is typically much shorter than the administrative validity period.

317.section: Art. Maastricht Treaty (1992), as amended by Lisbon (2009)
317.content: Treaty on European Union. One of the two core treaties of the EU (together with TFEU), establishing the fundamental principles, values, and objectives of the European Union. The TEU sets out the EU's institutional framework and provisions on common foreign and security policy. Article 4(3) establishes the principle of sincere cooperation between the EU and Member States.

318.content: Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. One of the two core treaties of the EU (together with TEU), establishing the constitutional basis for EU law. The TFEU lays down the competences, procedures, and institutions through which the EU exercises its powers. Key provisions include Article 114 (single market harmonisation, basis for eIDAS) and Article 218 (international agreements). Entered into force in 2009 with the Treaty of Lisbon.

319.content: A country that is not a member of the European Union. Third countries are relevant in the context of cross-border data transfers, recognition of trust services, and potential mutual recognition agreements for electronic identification.

320.content: a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or body other than the data subject, controller, processor and persons who, under the direct authority of the controller or processor, are authorised to process personal data

321.content: information that has been aggregated, transformed, analysed, interpreted or enriched to provide the necessary context for decision-making and to enable relevant and sufficient understanding in order to mitigate the impact of an ICT-related incident or of a cyber threat, including the technical details of a cyber-attack, those responsible for the attack and their modus operandi and motivations

322.content: a framework that mimics the tactics, techniques and procedures of real-life threat actors perceived as posing a genuine cyber threat, that delivers a controlled, bespoke, intelligence-led (red team) test of the financial entity’s critical live production systems

323.content: a trade repository as defined in Article 2, point (2), of Regulation (EU) No 648/2012

324.content: a trading venue as defined in Article 4(1), point (24), of Directive 2014/65/EU

325.content: any data processed for the purpose of the conveyance of a communication on an electronic communications network or for the billing thereof

326.content: the smallest unit of a work process within an electronic ledger | A discrete interaction between a user and another party, carried out through the European Digital Identity Wallet or within the broader scope of electronic identification and trust services. In the Regulation's title and subject-matter clause, the full phrase "electronic transaction" denotes the entire domain of interactions in the internal market that require secure electronic identification, authentication, or trust services (eIDAS Art. 1(b)); each individual wallet operation is a species of this broader category. In the EUDI Wallet context, the term takes on specific operational meaning: (1) dashboard logging — the wallet must provide "a log of all transactions" recording the time and date, counterpart identification, personal data requested, and data shared (eIDAS Art. 5a(4)(d); Reg. 2024/1183 Recital 13); each discrete wallet operation — issuance, presentation, signing, or pseudonym exchange — constitutes a logged transaction; (2) anti-tracking — providers of electronic attestations of attributes must prevent the collection of data that allows "transactions or user behaviour" to be tracked across relying parties (eIDAS Art. 5a(16)(a)); (3) intermediary data protection — intermediaries involved in the presentation of attestations of attributes shall not store data about the content of the transaction (eIDAS Art. 5b(10)); (4) liability — liability arises for failures "in a cross-border transaction" (eIDAS Art. 11a). In the ARF, the term takes on further technical precision: "remote presentation transaction flows" (ARF §4.4.3) and "Wallet-to-Wallet transaction flows" (ARF §6.6.4.2) describe specific protocol-level message exchanges for credential presentation.

327.section: Art. What is the related Trust Anchor?
327.content: As defined by RFC 5280, a Trust Anchor is the end point of a certificate validation process. As part of the EU Trusted List, when validating a qualified certificate, the Trust Anchor is the Service digital identity (Sdi) of a trust service entry (cf. ETSI TS 119 612 v2.1.1). | An authoritative entity represented by a public key and associated data. Trust anchors are the root of trust in a trust hierarchy, used to validate certificate chains and establish the authenticity of entities within the EUDI Wallet ecosystem.

328.content: an electronic service normally provided for remuneration which consists of any of the following: | a trust service as defined in Article 3, point (16), of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014

329.content: TSP a natural or a legal person who provides one or more trust services either as a qualified or as a non-qualified trust service provider | a trust service provider as defined in Article 3, point (19), of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 | A trust service provider (TSP) is a natural or a legal person who provides one or more trust services (TS) either as a qualified or as a non-qualified trust service provider. | A natural or a legal person who provides one or more trust services, either as a qualified or as a non-qualified trust service provider. Trust service providers (TSPs) form the backbone of the eIDAS trust infrastructure, offering services such as electronic signatures, seals, time stamps, registered delivery, website authentication certificates, and electronic attestations of attributes. Their obligations include: (1) taking appropriate technical and organisational measures to manage risks to the security of their services, and notifying the supervisory body and affected persons of any security breach without undue delay (eIDAS Art. 19); (2) where qualified, undergoing mandatory conformity assessments at least every 24 months (eIDAS Art. 20); (3) ensuring that qualified trust services are listed in national Trusted Lists (eIDAS Art. 22); (4) verifying the identity of applicants before issuing qualified certificates (eIDAS Art. 24(1)); and (5) in the EUDI Wallet context, identifying themselves to wallet units using wallet-relying party access certificates when issuing attestations (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 4(2)). Non-qualified TSPs are subject to lighter supervisory requirements but must still comply with baseline security and notification obligations. The distinction between qualified and non-qualified status determines the legal effect of services provided (eIDAS Art. 24 vs. Art. 19).

330.content: An isolated environment within a device's main processor designed to protect sensitive operations and data from the rest of the device's processing components, including the operating system and other applications. TEEs are often used in combination with secure elements to provide cryptographic isolation for wallet operations. While TEEs offer improved security over general-purpose environments, research has demonstrated that incorrectly designed TEEs may remain vulnerable to side-channel attacks.

331.section: Art. What is a Trusted List?
331.content: TL Each Member State shall establish, maintain and publish trusted lists, including information related to the qualified trust service providers for which it is responsible, together with information related to the qualified trust services provided by them. The information related to the trust services includes information about the status (e.g. granted, withdrawn) and the status history of the trust services in compliance with the applicable requirements and the relevant provisions of the eIDAS Regulation.

332.section: Art. What is the Trusted List Browser?
332.content: Trusted List Browser is a publicly available tool provided by the European Commission. It allows the user to browse through the information present in the Member States national Trusted Lists (TLs), as well as in the European Commission central list (named List of Trusted Lists (LOTL)). It provides an intuitive interface that is user-friendly and human-readable.

333.term: type of electronic attestation of attributes
333.termLower: type of electronic attestation of attributes
333.sectionTitle: type of electronic attestation of attributes
333.content: a specifically named and semantically described group of electronic attestation of attributes

334.section: Art. CJEU jurisprudence (Costa v. ENEL), EU Treaties
334.content: The legal framework of the European Union, comprising primary law (founding treaties) and secondary law (regulations, directives, decisions). Union law has supremacy over conflicting national law in areas where Member States have transferred competence to the EU. Regulations apply directly, while directives require transposition into national law.

335.content: A fixed legal phrase indicating that provisions from either EU-level legislation (Union law) or Member State domestic legislation (national law) may apply to a given situation. This formulation acknowledges the dual-layer legal structure of the EU, where both supranational and national rules may govern the same subject matter.

336.section: Art. Privacy research (Pfitzmann/Hansen terminology); EDPS TechDispatch #3/2025; eIDAS Article 5a(16)(b)
336.content: A privacy-preserving property ensuring that an observer cannot sufficiently determine whether multiple items of interest (such as attribute presentations, issuance sessions, or other wallet interactions) are related or originate from the same user. This prevents tracking and profiling of user behaviour. EDPS identifies four dimensions of unlinkability: (1) Unlinkability w.r.t. Relying Parties - RPs should not be able to determine whether multiple presentations correspond to the same user, even when colluding with other RPs; (2) Unlinkability w.r.t. Identity Providers - IdPs should not learn about wallet activity such as which RPs the user presents to (also called 'unobservability'); (3) Unlinkability w.r.t. Revocation Managers - entities managing credential status should not learn which RPs the wallet interacts with and when; (4) Unlinkability w.r.t. Colluding IdPs and RPs - presentations should remain unlinkable even when IdPs and RPs share information.

337.content: a natural or legal person, or a natural person representing another natural person or a legal person, that uses trust services or electronic identification means provided in accordance with this Regulation | any natural person using a publicly available electronic communications service, for private or business purposes, without necessarily having subscribed to this service

338.content: a transaction for which the required integrity, authenticity, and protocol-specific conditions have been checked in accordance with the governing rules of the distributed electronic ledger system

339.content: the process of verifying and confirming that data in electronic form are valid in accordance with this Regulation | The process of verifying and confirming that data in electronic form are valid in accordance with the eIDAS Regulation. In the EUDI Wallet ecosystem, validation is a multi-layered operation that occurs at several points: (1) wallet instance validation — the wallet verifies the wallet-relying party access certificate presented by relying parties or issuers, checking its authenticity, validity period, and revocation status before proceeding (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 4(2), 5(2)); (2) WUA validation — PID providers and attestation providers validate the wallet unit attestation during issuance to confirm they are interacting with a genuine, certified wallet unit (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 3); relying parties do not receive or validate WUAs directly but rely on transitive trust through the issuer's verification; (3) attestation validation — relying parties verify the cryptographic binding, issuer signatures/seals, validity period, and revocation status of PIDs and EAAs received from wallets (eIDAS Art. 5b(9), CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(3)); (4) signature/seal validation — qualified validation services for electronic signatures and seals confirm the qualified status and validity of signatures/seals at a given time (eIDAS Art. 33, 40); and (5) validation must be performed in accordance with the cryptographic standards listed in CIR 2024/2979 Annex II, using the trust anchors published in national Trusted Lists (eIDAS Art. 22).

340.content: data that is used to validate an electronic signature or an electronic seal

341.content: any service which requires the processing of traffic data or location data other than traffic data beyond what is necessary for the transmission of a communication or the billing thereof

342.section: Art. W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0
342.content: VC A tamper-evident credential that has authorship that can be cryptographically verified. Verifiable credentials can be used to represent information found in physical credentials such as passports, licenses, and diplomas. In the EUDI Wallet ecosystem, PIDs and attestations are issued as verifiable credentials following the W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model or ISO mDL standards.

343.section: Art. W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model
343.content: An entity that requests and receives verifiable credentials or presentations from a Holder, then validates the cryptographic proofs and attribute claims. In the EUDI Wallet ecosystem, Verifiers are typically Relying Parties, but in wallet-to-wallet interactions, another Wallet User can act as a Verifier.

344.content: A Wallet Unit used by a Verifier in the context of Wallet-to-Wallet interactions. The Verifier Wallet Unit requests and receives PIDs or attestations from a Holder Wallet Unit.

345.content: a weakness, susceptibility or flaw of an asset, system, process or control that can be exploited | a weakness, susceptibility or flaw of ICT products or ICT services that can be exploited by a cyber threat

346.content: a cryptographic mechanism necessary in the context of authentication of the wallet user and the issuance or presentation of person identification data or electronic attestations of attributes

347.content: the application installed and configured on a wallet user’s device or environment, which is part of a wallet unit, and that the wallet user uses to interact with the wallet unit | the application installed and configured on a wallet user’s device or environment, which is part of a wallet unit, and that the wallet user uses to interact with the wallet unit | the application installed and configured on a wallet user’s device or environment, which is part of a wallet unit, and that the wallet user uses to interact with the wallet unit | the application installed and configured on a wallet user’s device or environment, which is part of a wallet unit, and that the wallet user uses to interact with the wallet unit | the application installed and configured on a wallet user’s device or environment, which is part of a wallet unit, and that the wallet user uses to interact with the wallet unit | the application installed and configured on a wallet user’s device or environment, which is part of a wallet unit, and that the wallet user uses to interact with the wallet unit | the application installed and configured on a wallet user’s device or environment, which is part of a wallet unit, and that the wallet user uses to interact with the wallet unit | the application installed and configured on a wallet user’s device or environment, which is part of a wallet unit, and that the wallet user uses to interact with the wallet unit | the application installed and configured on a wallet user’s device or environment, which is part of a wallet unit, and which the wallet user uses to interact with the wallet unit | The application installed and configured on a wallet user's device or environment, which is part of a wallet unit (together with a WSCA and WSCD), and that the wallet user uses to interact with the wallet unit. The wallet instance serves as the primary interface for all wallet operations: (1) it presents wallet unit attestations (WUAs) to PID providers and attestation providers during issuance for trust establishment (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 3) — WUAs are not presented to relying parties (ARF §6.5.3.4, AS-WP-09-030); (2) it manages the issuance flow for receiving person identification data and electronic attestations of attributes, verifying that issuers hold valid wallet-relying party access certificates before accepting credentials (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 4(2)); (3) it handles attribute presentation (both remote and proximity), ensuring selective disclosure and user consent (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5); (4) it interfaces with the WSCA, which in turn uses the WSCD, to perform cryptographic operations such as signing, key generation, and proof-of-possession (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 4-5); (5) it maintains the transaction dashboard where users review interaction logs and manage their credentials (CIR 2024/2980); and (6) it supports qualified electronic signature and seal creation by interfacing with local, external, or remote QSCDs (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 12). The wallet provider must ensure the integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality of communication between wallet instances and WSCAs (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 4(2)).

348.content: a natural or legal person who provides wallet solutions | a natural or legal person who provides wallet solutions | a natural or legal person who provides wallet solutions | a natural or legal person who provides wallet solutions | a natural or legal person who provides wallet solutions | a natural or legal person who provides wallet solutions | a natural or legal person who provides wallet solutions | a natural or legal person who provides wallet solutions | a natural or legal person who provides wallet solutions | A natural or legal person who provides wallet solutions and bears end-to-end responsibility for the lifecycle of every wallet unit issued under those solutions. Wallet providers must obtain certification of their wallet solutions under national certification schemes before deployment (CIR 2024/2981). Their core obligations include: (1) issuing and signing wallet unit attestations (WUAs) for each wallet unit, using certificates listed in the Trusted List (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 3(2), 6); (2) ensuring the integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality of communication between wallet instances and wallet secure cryptographic applications (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 4(2)); (3) guaranteeing that wallet units support standard protocols and interfaces for PID and EAA issuance, attribute presentation (both remote and proximity), selective disclosure, data erasure requests, and relying party reporting (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 3-8); (4) maintaining transaction logs with integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality, and enabling wallet users to export logged information (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 10); (5) being the sole entity capable of revoking WUAs, with obligations to publish revocation status in a privacy-preserving manner and inform affected users within 24 hours (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 7); (6) ensuring wallet users who are natural persons have free-of-charge access to signature creation applications for non-professional purposes (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 12(3)); and (7) processing embedded disclosure policies attached to attestations (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 11).

349.content: WSCA an application that manages critical assets by being linked to and using the cryptographic and non-cryptographic functions provided by the wallet secure cryptographic device | an application that manages critical assets by being linked to and using the cryptographic and non-cryptographic functions provided by the wallet secure cryptographic device | an application that manages critical assets by being linked to and using the cryptographic and non-cryptographic functions provided by the wallet secure cryptographic device | an application that manages critical assets by being linked to and using the cryptographic and non-cryptographic functions provided by the wallet secure cryptographic device | an application that manages critical assets by being linked to and using the cryptographic and non-cryptographic functions provided by the wallet secure cryptographic device | an application that manages critical assets by being linked to and using the cryptographic and non-cryptographic functions provided by the wallet secure cryptographic device | an application that manages critical assets by being linked to and using the cryptographic and non-cryptographic functions provided by the wallet secure cryptographic device | an application that manages critical assets by being linked to and using the cryptographic and non-cryptographic functions provided by the wallet secure cryptographic device | an application that manages critical assets by being linked to and using the cryptographic and non-cryptographic functions provided by the wallet secure cryptographic device | An application that manages critical assets by being linked to and using the cryptographic and non-cryptographic functions provided by the wallet secure cryptographic device (WSCD). The WSCA is the software layer that mediates between the wallet instance and the WSCD, orchestrating all security-critical operations. Its key roles include: (1) managing cryptographic keys — requesting key generation within the WSCD, maintaining references to keys, and invoking signing and decryption operations (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 4-5); (2) protecting critical assets beyond just keys, including wallet unit attestation data, user authentication secrets, and attestation-binding proofs (CIR 2024/2979 Rec. 6); (3) supporting the presentation of electronic attestations of attributes, which is identified as a crucial WSCA functionality (CIR 2024/2979 Rec. 6); (4) being subject to certification under national certification schemes, where it must demonstrate resistance against attackers with high attack potential (CIR 2024/2981 Annex IV); (5) when provided as a Java Card applet to embedded secure elements, following the technical specifications listed in CIR 2024/2979 Annex I (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 4(2)); and (6) the wallet provider must ensure the integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality of all communication between wallet instances and WSCAs (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 4(2)).

350.content: WSCD a tamper-resistant device that provides an environment that is linked to and used by the wallet secure cryptographic application to protect critical assets and provide cryptographic functions for the secure execution of critical operations | a tamper-resistant device that provides an environment that is linked to and used by the wallet secure cryptographic application to protect critical assets and provide cryptographic functions for the secure execution of critical operations | a tamper-resistant device that provides an environment that is linked to and used by the wallet secure cryptographic application to protect critical assets and provide cryptographic functions for the secure execution of critical operations | a tamper-resistant device that provides an environment that is linked to and used by the wallet secure cryptographic application to protect critical assets and provide cryptographic functions for the secure execution of critical operations | a tamper-resistant device that provides an environment that is linked to and used by the wallet secure cryptographic application to protect critical assets and provide cryptographic functions for the secure execution of critical operations | a tamper-resistant device that provides an environment that is linked to and used by the wallet secure cryptographic application to protect critical assets and provide cryptographic functions for the secure execution of critical operations | a tamper-resistant device that provides an environment that is linked to and used by the wallet secure cryptographic application to protect critical assets and provide cryptographic functions for the secure execution of critical operations | a tamper-resistant device that provides an environment that is linked to and used by the wallet secure cryptographic application to protect critical assets and provide cryptographic functions for the secure execution of critical operations | a tamper-resistant device that provides an environment that is linked to and used by the wallet secure cryptographic application to protect critical assets and provide cryptographic functions for the secure execution of critical operations | A tamper-resistant device that provides an environment that is linked to and used by the wallet secure cryptographic application (WSCA) to protect critical assets and provide cryptographic functions for the secure execution of critical operations. The WSCD is the hardware root of trust in the EUDI Wallet architecture. Its key properties and requirements include: (1) it protects cryptographic private keys throughout their entire lifecycle — generation, storage, and use — such that private keys are never exposed outside the WSCD boundary (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 4-5); (2) it must be resistant to attackers with high attack potential, as assessed under the requirements of assurance level high in Implementing Regulation 2015/1502 (CIR 2024/2981 Annex IV); (3) it must be certified to at least Common Criteria EAL4 with advanced methodical vulnerability analysis comparable to AVA_VAN.5, or equivalent (CIR 2024/2981 Rec. 7); (4) it may take several physical forms including embedded secure elements (eSE) in user devices, external smartcards, or remote HSM-based implementations (ARF Topic 9); (5) when not provided by the wallet provider (e.g. an eSE embedded in the user's phone), the wallet solution must establish and verify assumptions about the WSCD's security properties as part of its certification (CIR 2024/2981 Annex IV); and (6) cryptographic operations performed in the WSCD are not required to be fully self-contained, but the WSCD must guarantee protection of those operations against high-potential attacks (CIR 2024/2981 Annex IV).

352.content: WU a unique configuration of a wallet solution that includes wallet instances, wallet secure cryptographic applications and wallet secure cryptographic devices provided by a wallet provider to an individual wallet user | a unique configuration of a wallet solution that includes wallet instances, wallet secure cryptographic applications and wallet secure cryptographic devices provided by a wallet provider to an individual wallet user | a unique configuration of a wallet solution that includes wallet instances, wallet secure cryptographic applications and wallet secure cryptographic devices provided by a wallet provider to an individual wallet user | a unique configuration of a wallet solution that includes wallet instances, wallet secure cryptographic applications and wallet secure cryptographic devices provided by a wallet provider to an individual wallet user | a unique configuration of a wallet solution that includes wallet instances, wallet secure cryptographic applications and wallet secure cryptographic devices provided by a wallet provider to an individual wallet user | a unique configuration of a wallet solution that includes wallet instances, wallet secure cryptographic applications and wallet secure cryptographic devices provided by a wallet provider to an individual wallet user | a unique configuration of a wallet solution that includes wallet instances, wallet secure cryptographic applications and wallet secure cryptographic devices provided by a wallet provider to an individual wallet user | a unique configuration of a wallet solution that includes wallet instances, wallet secure cryptographic applications and wallet secure cryptographic devices provided by a wallet provider to an individual wallet user | a unique configuration of a wallet solution that includes wallet instances, wallet secure cryptographic applications and wallet secure cryptographic devices provided by a wallet provider to an individual wallet user

353.content: WUA a data object that describes the components of the wallet unit or allows authentication and validation of those components | a data object that describes the components of the wallet unit or allows authentication and validation of those components | a data object that describes the components of the wallet unit or allows authentication and validation of those components | a data object that describes the components of the wallet unit or allows authentication and validation of those components | A cryptographically signed or sealed data object, issued by the Wallet Provider for each Wallet Unit, that describes the components of the wallet unit and enables authentication and validation of those components. The WUA is a JWT containing public keys (whose corresponding private keys are protected by a WSCD), a revocation handle (status list URI + index), and an eudi_wallet_info claim with general_info (wallet provider name, solution ID, version, certification info) and key_storage_info (storage type, certification). It is signed using a certificate listed in the Trusted List. The WUA is presented only to PID Providers and Attestation Providers during issuance via OID4VCI (as a key_attestation element in the CredentialRequest), enabling them to verify that they are issuing credentials to a genuine, certified wallet unit and to make informed decisions about key binding based on WSCA/WSCD capabilities. To ensure User privacy, the Wallet Unit does not present the WUA to Relying Parties (ARF §6.5.3.4); data related to the User device must not be released to them (AS-WP-09-030). Instead, Relying Parties verify the Wallet Unit indirectly through transitive trust: the PID/attestation signature (verified against the Provider Trusted List), device key binding (mdoc DeviceAuth or SD-JWT Key Binding JWT), and cascaded revocation (if a WUA is revoked, the PID Provider must revoke the PID per CIR 2024/2977 Art. 5(4)(b)). Only the Wallet Provider may revoke a WUA, and privacy-preserving techniques (such as once-only attestations, batch issuance, or limited lifetimes) must be employed to prevent colluding PID Providers or Attestation Providers from correlating WUA presentations across issuance sessions (ARF Topic A).

354.content: a user who is in control of the wallet unit | a user who is in control of the wallet unit | a user who is in control of the wallet unit | a user who is in control of the wallet unit | a user who is in control of the wallet unit | a user who is in control of the wallet unit | a user who is in control of the wallet unit | a user who is in control of the wallet unit | a user who is in control of the wallet unit | A user who is in control of the wallet unit — the natural or legal person (or a natural person representing another) who operates a wallet unit to store, manage, and present person identification data and electronic attestations of attributes. The wallet user's rights and protections include: (1) full control over which attributes are shared with relying parties, with the ability to selectively disclose a subset of attributes from any PID or attestation (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(4)); (2) the right to request erasure of personal data from relying parties via standardised wallet interfaces (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 6, GDPR Art. 17); (3) the ability to report relying parties to data protection authorities directly through the wallet dashboard (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 7); (4) access to a transaction log recording all interactions, with the ability to export logged data (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 10); (5) transparent notification within 24 hours if their wallet unit attestation is revoked by the wallet provider, including the reason and consequences (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 7(3)); (6) the right to verify the identity and registration status of relying parties before sharing data (eIDAS Art. 5a(4)(a), Art. 5b(8)); and (7) free-of-charge access to qualified electronic signature creation for non-professional purposes (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 12(3), eIDAS Art. 5a(2)).

355.content: WRP a relying party that intends to rely upon wallet units for the provision of public or private services by means of digital interaction | a relying party that intends to rely upon wallet units for the provision of public or private services by means of digital interaction | a relying party that intends to rely upon wallet units for the provision of public or private services by means of digital interaction | a relying party that intends to rely upon wallet units for the provision of public or private services by means of digital interaction | a relying party that intends to rely upon wallet units for the provision of public or private services by means of digital interaction | a relying party that intends to rely upon wallet units for the provision of public or private services by means of digital interaction | A relying party that intends to rely upon wallet units. This term distinguishes entities that interact specifically with EUDI Wallets from the broader eIDAS concept of relying party. Wallet-relying parties encompass three functional roles: (1) PID providers that issue person identification data to wallet units (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 2(1)); (2) attestation providers that issue electronic attestations of attributes (including QEAAs and PuB-EAAs) to wallet units (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 2(1)); and (3) verifiers that request and validate attributes from wallet units during presentation flows (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5). All wallet-relying parties must: register with their Member State (eIDAS Art. 5b(1)); obtain a wallet-relying party access certificate from a mandated provider (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 3(12-13)); authenticate themselves to wallet units using that certificate (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(2)); and comply with embedded disclosure policies attached to attestations (CIR 2024/2979 Art. 11). The wallet must enable its user to verify the identity of the wallet-relying party before proceeding with any data exchange (eIDAS Art. 5a(4)(a), CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(5)).

356.content: a certificate for electronic seals or signatures authenticating and validating the wallet-relying party issued by a provider of wallet-relying party access certificates | a certificate for electronic seals or signatures authenticating and validating the wallet-relying party issued by a provider of wallet-relying party access certificates | a certificate for electronic seals or signatures authenticating and validating the wallet-relying party issued by a provider of wallet-relying party access certificates | a certificate for electronic seals or signatures authenticating and validating the wallet-relying party issued by a provider of wallet-relying party access certificates | a certificate for electronic seals or signatures authenticating and validating the wallet-relying party issued by a provider of wallet-relying party access certificates | A certificate for electronic seals or signatures authenticating and validating the wallet-relying party, issued by a provider of wallet-relying party access certificates. These certificates are the trust anchor through which relying parties prove their identity and authorisation to wallet units during all interactions. Key aspects include: (1) they are mandatory — any entity wishing to request attributes from or issue attestations to a wallet unit must present a valid access certificate (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 3(12), CIR 2024/2982 Art. 2(10-11)); (2) they are issued exclusively by providers mandated by Member States (access certificate authorities), creating a government-anchored chain of trust (CIR 2024/2977 Art. 3(13)); (3) the certificate must contain the relying party's registered identity and the specific attributes they are authorised to request, enabling the wallet to enforce data minimisation at the protocol level (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(2)); (4) wallet instances must verify the validity and revocation status of access certificates before accepting issuance requests or sharing attributes (CIR 2024/2982 Art. 4(2), 5(2)); and (5) the technical format and content requirements for access certificates are specified in CIR 2024/2977 Art. 3 and the standards listed in CIR 2024/2979 Annex II.

358.content: A legal phrase indicating that a provision applies only in certain circumstances or to certain entities. It creates conditional applicability, meaning the requirement only takes effect when the relevant conditions are met. Used to provide flexibility for diverse situations across Member States.

359.content: A legal phrase meaning "this provision applies, but it does not affect, override, or diminish the rights, obligations, or provisions established by [the referenced provision]." It signals that both rules coexist and the referenced provision maintains its full force. Example: "Without prejudice to paragraph 1" means paragraph 1 still fully applies.

360.content: A legal phrase requiring action as soon as reasonably possible under the circumstances, without unnecessary or unjustified postponement. It imposes a flexible but enforceable time obligation, allowing for reasonable delays caused by circumstances beyond control. Often paired with a maximum deadline: "without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours."

361.content: one or more sequences of actions required to produce an outcome that complies with governing rules of an electronic ledger

362.section: Art. Which signature format should I use?
362.content: XML advanced electronic signature (XAdES), based on XML signatures. XML documents are suggested to be signed/sealed using XAdES signature format (either with enveloped or enveloping packaging).

363.content: ZKP A cryptographic method by which one party (the prover) can prove to another party (the verifier) that a statement is true, without revealing any information beyond the validity of the statement itself. In the EUDIW context, ZKPs can enable proving properties about attributes (e.g., "age is over 18") without disclosing the actual attribute value.

364.content: This Directive provides for the harmonisation of the national provisions required to ensure an equivalent level of protection of fundamental rights and freedoms, and in particular the right to privacy and confidentiality, with respect to the processing of personal data in the electronic communication sector and to ensure the free movement of such data and of electronic communication equipment and services in the Community.

365.content: Save as otherwise provided, the definitions in Directive 95/46/EC and in Directive 2002/21/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 March 2002 on a common regulatory framework for electronic communications networks and services (Framework Directive) ( 8 ) shall apply.

366.content: This Directive shall apply to the processing of personal data in connection with the provision of publicly available electronic communications services in public communications networks in the Community, including public communications networks supporting data collection and identification devices.

367.content: The provider of a publicly available electronic communications service must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to safeguard security of its services, if necessary in conjunction with the provider of the public communications network with respect to network security. Having regard to the state of the art and the cost of their implementation, these measures shall ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk presented.

368.content: Member States shall ensure the confidentiality of communications and the related traffic data by means of a public communications network and publicly available electronic communications services, through national legislation. In particular, they shall prohibit listening, tapping, storage or other kinds of interception or surveillance of communications and the related traffic data by persons other than users, without the consent of the users concerned, except when legally authorised to do so in accordance with Article 15(1). This paragraph shall not prevent technical storage which is necessary for the conveyance of a communication without prejudice to the principle of confidentiality.

369.content: Traffic data relating to subscribers and users processed and stored by the provider of a public communications network or publicly available electronic communications service must be erased or made anonymous when it is no longer needed for the purpose of the transmission of a communication without prejudice to paragraphs 2, 3 and 5 of this Article and Article 15(1).

370.content: Subscribers shall have the right to receive non-itemised bills.

371.sectionTitle: Presentation and restriction of calling and connected line identification
371.content: Where presentation of calling line identification is offered, the service provider must offer the calling user the possibility, using a simple means and free of charge, of preventing the presentation of the calling line identification on a per-call basis.
